# Excel Automation V1.05 - Performance Benchmark Report

**Methodology**: a single mock `.xlsx` file (`backend/scripts/bench_300k.xlsx`, generated by
`scripts/make_mock.py`) with **300,474 input rows** (8,500 PPIDs, 46,586 `TS#` blocks / output
rows, 6.59 MB) was run through the transformation pipeline in-process (no HTTP/network overhead)
using `backend/scripts/benchmark.py`. Peak memory was sampled on a 20ms-interval background
thread tracking process RSS (captures native pandas/numpy/calamine buffer allocations that
`tracemalloc`'s Python-heap-only tracking would miss). Each configuration was run 3+ times; the
measurements below are representative of the stable, repeated numbers (see "A note on
measurement variance" for the one place this needed extra care).

## Headline comparison

| Metric | V1.04.1 (baseline) | V1.05 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total processing time | 15.24 s | 1.77 s | **8.6x faster** |
| Rows processed / second | 19,713 | 169,409 | **8.6x** |
| Peak memory | 285.0 MB | 338.5 MB | +18.8% (see below) |
| Read + parse stage | 11.47 s | 1.53 s | **7.5x faster** |
| Transform stage | 0.32 s | 0.24 s | ~25% faster |
| xlsx write stage | 3.44 s | *(eliminated)* | -100% |

Raw data: `backend/scripts/bench_result_V1.04.json`, `backend/scripts/bench_result_V1.05.json`.

## Optimization summary

1. **Removed the unused xlsx write from `/api/convert`** (`backend/app/api/routes.py`,
   `models/schemas.py`). V1.04's `ConvertResponse` included a base64-encoded `.xlsx` on every
   conversion, but the frontend's Download button was already calling the separate, stateless
   `/api/export` endpoint with client-side `rows` data - `file_base64` was dead weight on the
   wire. Confirmed unused via `grep` across the whole frontend before removing it. This alone
   eliminated the 3.44s xlsx-write stage (23% of V1.04's total time) from every conversion.
2. **Adopted `python-calamine` (Rust-based) as the primary `.xlsx`/`.xls` reader**, replacing
   openpyxl/xlrd as the hot path (they remain as an automatic fallback - see Reliability). This
   was the single biggest win: the read+parse stage dropped from ~11-20s to ~1.5s for the same
   300k-row file. Before adopting it, calamine's output was validated to be byte-and-type-identical
   to openpyxl/xlrd across 6 scenarios (standard file, legacy `.xls`, this 300k-row file, a real
   Excel-COM-saved `.xls`, Korean/CJK text, and numeric/blank-cell edge cases) - see
   `backend/tests/test_calamine_equivalence.py`. Per explicit instruction, this was only adopted
   after that validation passed, with a documented fallback for anything outside the validated
   scenarios.
3. **Columnar (dict-of-lists) `DataFrame` construction** in `ExcelTransformer._to_dataframe`,
   replacing a list of ~46,586 individual per-row `dict` objects. Pandas builds each column
   directly from its own list instead of introspecting every row-dict for its keys - a modest
   (~25%) but real improvement, and the already-fast transform stage was never the bottleneck.
4. **`read_only=True` for the openpyxl fallback path** - only ~3% faster than default mode on its
   own (see "what didn't work" below), but kept because it's essentially free and reduces memory
   for the (now rarely-taken) fallback path.

## Bottleneck analysis

At V1.04.1, reading and parsing the `.xlsx` file was **75% of total processing time** - by far
the dominant cost, not the PPID/TS# grouping logic (which was already fast: 0.32s for 300k rows).
Writing the result back out as `.xlsx` on every conversion (needed for nothing, since downloads
go through a separate endpoint) was the second-largest cost at 23%. Together these two issues
accounted for ~98% of V1.04's total processing time - which is exactly what V1.05 targeted.

**What didn't work as well as expected**: the first optimization attempted was
`engine_kwargs={"read_only": True}` for openpyxl, expecting a large win from avoiding the full
in-memory workbook object model. Measured back-to-back on the same file, it was only ~3% faster
than default mode (20.4s vs 19.8s average of 3 runs) - openpyxl's fundamental bottleneck is its
Python-level cell-by-cell XML parsing, which `read_only` mode doesn't change enough to matter at
this scale. This is why calamine (a different, Rust-based parser) was evaluated next, and it's
the change that actually delivered the target improvement.

## The memory trade-off, honestly

Peak memory went **up** (285.0 MB -> 338.5 MB, +18.8%), not down, despite "reduce peak memory
usage" being a stated V1.05 objective. This deserves a direct explanation rather than being
glossed over:

- Isolating just the read step: calamine peaks at ~338 MB vs. ~245 MB for openpyxl in
  `read_only` mode, for the same file. Calamine's Rust implementation appears to materialize more
  of the sheet at once rather than streaming as conservatively as openpyxl's read-only generator
  does - it trades memory for a dramatically faster single pass.
- In absolute terms, 338.5 MB for a 300k-row file is not a practical concern on any modern server
  (nowhere near causing memory pressure or OOM risk) - and a slow, blocking 15-20s request is a
  worse reliability/UX risk in practice (request timeouts, a frozen-feeling UI, tied-up worker
  threads) than an extra ~90 MB of RAM for the few seconds a conversion takes.
- The fallback path (openpyxl `read_only`) is still fully wired up and automatically used if
  calamine ever fails on a given file, so the lower-memory path already exists as a safety net -
  it just isn't the default, because speed was judged the higher priority for this app's actual
  usage pattern (interactive, one-file-at-a-time conversions, not a batch memory-constrained
  environment).

This is a conscious, documented trade-off (see `excel_io.py`'s `_read_excel_binary` docstring),
not an oversight. If a future deployment context genuinely needs the lower-memory profile (e.g.
many concurrent conversions on a memory-constrained host), the existing fallback engine could be
promoted back to the default via a one-line change - the architecture already supports it.

## A note on measurement variance

Early ad hoc timing (outside the final benchmark harness) showed real run-to-run variance for the
openpyxl read step - anywhere from ~11s to ~20s for the identical file and code, on this specific
development machine. This is a known characteristic of the development environment (an external
USB SSD with occasional I/O variability, not a network drive as initially suspected - confirmed
via `Get-PSDrive`). The final headline numbers above come from the same `benchmark.py` harness run
back-to-back for both V1.04 and V1.05 configurations, minimizing (though not eliminating) this
effect; the *relative* improvement (8.6x) was consistently reproduced across every repeated run
regardless of the absolute baseline number that run happened to show.

## Frontend / large-dataset preview

AG Grid Community (already in use since V1.03) virtualizes row rendering, so the preview grid's
DOM footprint doesn't grow with row count. This was not independently load-tested against a
synthetic 46,000+ row rendered grid in this session (no browser automation tool was available in
this environment) - it's an architectural expectation from AG Grid's virtualization, not a
directly measured guarantee. Recommended for V1.06: an actual browser-based load test at the
46k-row scale this app now produces from a 300k-row input file.
